title: Gymnastics Coach Who Filmed Minors In Bathroom Gets Maximum 90 Years
desc:
Gymnastics Coach Who Filmed Minors In Bathroom Gets Maximum 90 Years

A federal judge in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, sentenced former youth gymnastics coach Sean Gardner, 39, to the maximum 90 years in prison on Oct. 14. U.S. District Judge Kristi Johnson gave him 30 years on each of three federal counts of producing child sexual abuse material, a term that amounts to life.

Gardner pleaded guilty to hiding a camera in a bathroom at a gym in Purvis, Mississippi, between December 2017 and April 2018. The Justice Department says he secretly videotaped gymnasts in the restroom of the gym where he coached. He had been indicted on 10 counts in August 2025, and a superseding indictment in April added two more. He pleaded to counts 1, 3 and 7, and KCRG reported the plea in May.

Investigators say the recordings show at least 10 minors undressing or naked, and that they turned up only years later, when police were looking into abuse allegations against him in Iowa. An FBI affidavit cited by CBS News says agents seized about 50 videos and 400 photos from his residence. West Des Moines police searched his apartment in May 2025, and the FBI arrested him that August.

Gardner has not been charged over the Iowa allegations. Police told CBS they will decide how to proceed once the federal case ends. Court records cited by NBC News say at least three young gymnasts at Chow's Gymnastics and Dance Institute, the West Des Moines gym where he worked from 2018 to 2022, were sexually abused. Those are allegations, and nothing in the Iowa records has been tested in court.

Sean Gardner was just sentenced to 90 years in prison for secretly recording young gymnasts undressing in a locker room at a gym in Mississippi. Gardner also had coached at Chow's Gym, owned by Liang "Chow" Qiao (who coached Shawn Johnson to Olympic gold). Reportedly Chow knew of abuse allegations and failed to report them for years. Former USA Gymnastics leader Li Li Leung was just awarded the 2026 Torch Award from the USOPC for her leadership and impact on the Olympic movements. Why is gymnastics STILL such a grotesque shit show of abuse??? And seriously, would you let this guy anywhere near your daughter?

— Jennifer Sey (@JenniferSey) October 15, 2026

Two lawsuits filed Dec. 1 in Polk County, Iowa, say USA Gymnastics and SafeSport were told about Gardner's behavior in December 2017. The plaintiffs are two former gymnasts. According to AP's account of the filings, the suits allege the organizations were alerted to "inappropriate and abusive behaviors" at the Mississippi gym, did not investigate, did not revoke his credentials and did not go to police. They say that inaction let him land the Iowa job. The suits also name Chow's and its founder, Liang "Chow" Qiao, and they remain pending.

SafeSport disputes the timeline. It told AP it first heard of sexual misconduct allegations against Gardner in 2022 and acted swiftly from there. It says USA Gymnastics told it in January 2018 only that an affiliated gym had resolved a report involving him, and it did not dig further because the report was not about sexual misconduct and lacked detail. CBS reports that Gardner's boss in Mississippi said in an email that she told USA Gymnastics about his "grooming behavior" in January 2018. AP reported that USA Gymnastics and SafeSport declined to comment on the litigation, and that Gardner's lawyer did not respond.

What happened after 2022 is harder to square with its account. It suspended Gardner provisionally in July 2022, four months after a girl first reported him to the center, and Chow's fired him. Yet AP reported he took a hospital job in May 2024 while still under suspension. Three people familiar with the case told AP that Gardner was willing in early 2025 to accept a lifetime coaching ban, and that SafeSport never finalized it. SafeSport said it took swift action and that temporary and permanent bans carry the same restrictions.

SafeSport's own investigation found that Chow and other coaches at the Iowa gym knew of the allegations and did not report them as policy requires, per OutKick. Police records say a detective asked SafeSport to encourage families to file criminal complaints, but only one parent contacted police in 2022, and that investigation stalled. Chow's and Qiao did not respond to AP when Gardner was arrested.

Gardner's career ran through three states. The FBI says he coached at Athletes in Motion in Prairieville, Louisiana, from 2004 to 2014, at Jump'In Gymnastics in Purvis from 2014 to 2018, and at Chow's from 2018 to 2022. Agents opened a website for possible victims after the arrest, saying he mainly targeted children at gyms in all three states.

His plea did not waive his right to appeal. The civil suits against him, USA Gymnastics, SafeSport and the Iowa gym are still pending. The case revives questions about SafeSport that surfaced after the Larry Nassar scandal.

title: Whitmer Declares Energy Emergency, Eases Diesel Rules For Farmers
desc:
Whitmer Declares Energy Emergency, Eases Diesel Rules For Farmers

Authored by Kimberly Hayek via The Epoch Times,

Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer declared a state of energy emergency on Oct. 12, citing disruptions to global oil markets from the war in Iran and what she said was the nation's largest year-over-year rise in average gasoline prices in Michigan.

The order allows certain farm and logging vehicles to use dyed diesel on public roads.

In her emergency order, Whitmer said that Michigan's farmers and loggers are facing record-high diesel prices, slim margins, and sharp market swings, with some costs passed on to consumers.

"These industries already purchase and maintain substantial supplies of dyed diesel for off-road equipment. Therefore, granting eligible highway-licensed vehicles temporary access to this fuel would provide immediate relief," she wrote.

Her order suspends specific provisions of the Motor Fuel Tax Act that normally bar such use of dyed diesel.

Global Supply Shrinks

Armed conflicts have tightened crude oil supply, driving up prices for both diesel and regular gasoline.

The hostilities with Iran, which began at the end of February, have slowed shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the point through which about 25 percent of the seaborne oil trade used to flow, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). Shortly after the conflict started in March, diesel prices saw their biggest one-week jump on record.

Global diesel markets could remain tight well into next year, with resulting high prices driving inflation and hurting economic growth, as conflicts curb output from the Middle East and Russia, the agency said on Oct. 14.

Combined diesel export losses from the Middle East and Russia totaled 1.3 million barrels per day in September, the agency said.

Pump Prices Bite

The average pump price for a gallon of regular gasoline in the United States was $4.33 per gallon as of Oct. 14, according to the American Automobile Association. Diesel is much higher, at about $6.30 per gallon, reaching a record high of $6.52 at the end of last month.

The emergency order ends when the governor determines the shortage no longer exists, but no later than Dec. 31. Willful interference with the order is a misdemeanor.

Whitmer noted she had issued an earlier order in April that suspended Reid vapor-pressure requirements in gasoline and temporarily lowered consumer prices. She wrote that the federal government created the problem and can fix it.

Whitmer, a Democrat, is term-limited. Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, a Democrat, and Rep. John James (R-Mich.) clashed over tariffs on Canada, the war in Iran, and Medicaid in the first debate of the race for Michigan governor on Oct. 6.

Benson blamed the war in Iran for rising fuel prices and said James had voted six times to support the war. Both candidates said they would support suspending Michigan's gas tax.

Michigan has faced prior fuel-supply disruptions. In 2022, Whitmer declared an energy emergency after a refinery fire in Indiana, temporarily easing certain transport and fuel rules.

title: Iowa Attorney General Sues Camera Company Over Ties To China
desc:
Iowa Attorney General Sues Camera Company Over Ties To China

Authored by Frank Fang via The Epoch Times,

Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird has filed a lawsuit against home security camera maker Lorex, alleging the company used deceptive business practices to mislead consumers about potential security risks tied to its products.

The complaint, announced by Bird's office on Oct. 9, alleges that Lorex "hid material facts" from consumers and that information collected by its products "is susceptible to being accessed by China and the Chinese Communist Party."

Iowa is not the first state to take legal action against Lorex. Nebraska, Texas, and Missouri have also filed similar lawsuits against the company.

At the center of the lawsuit is Lorex's connection to Zhejiang Dahua Technology, a Chinese surveillance equipment maker on the Pentagon's blacklist of Chinese military companies.

Although Lorex's ownership has since changed from Dahua to Taiwan-based Skywatch, the complaint alleges that the company "still markets and sells" some camera products "made using components and technology" from Dahua.

"The fact that a Chinese-backed company can spy on Iowa kids and families through baby cameras is creepy and scary," Bird said in a statement on Oct. 9.

"Iowa parents want to be sure their baby is getting a good, safe night's sleep. They shouldn't have to worry that the Chinese government can also view that footage.

"Enough is enough - China needs to stay out of our homes. Companies like Lorex that help China access Iowans private data will be held accountable to Iowa law."

The complaint cites China's 2017 National Intelligence Law, which it says raises concerns that Beijing could access data collected by Lorex cameras.

A provision requires organizations and citizens to "support, assist, and cooperate with national intelligence efforts."

The law "forms the baseline of the modern data collection regime," according to the complaint, which cites the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

It also creates "a legal obligation for those entities to turn over data collected abroad and domestically" to Beijing, the complaint states.

The complaint also warns that China's 2021 Regulations on the Management of Security Vulnerabilities in Network Products could let Chinese authorities learn of security flaws before companies can issue patches to fix them.

The 2017 law and 2021 regulations call into question Lorex's assurances that its cameras are "private by design" and that it takes "every step possible to ensure your recordings remain private," the complaint says.

Another practice the lawsuit accuses Lorex of using to mislead consumers is a disclaimer on its frequently asked questions page.

In a question addressing the 2019 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), Lorex states that its products "are designed for consumer and business use only and not for U.S. federal governments, federally-funded projects or contractors subject to NDAA."

While Lorex's statement acknowledges that the products are restricted from federal use, the complaint argues that the company's disclaimer "reflects Lorex's actual knowledge of the security concerns associated with its products but provides no explanation of why the disclaimer is significant."

The complaint states, "A consumer would interpret the disclaimer as stating that any concern is limited to federal government use, and therefore that Lorex cameras are safe for household and business use. The disclaimer is therefore misleading."

Bird is seeking reimbursement, civil penalties, and fees from Lorex for violating Iowa's Consumer Fraud Act, according to her office.

The Epoch Times contacted Lorex for comments and didn't receive a response by publication time.

Bird has filed two other China-related lawsuits recently.

On Oct. 7, Bird announced a lawsuit against video surveillance company ADI Global Distribution, alleging it concealed that its cameras were manufactured in China by Hikvision and Dahua.

Hikvision is also on the Pentagon's blacklist of Chinese military companies.

A day earlier, Bird announced a lawsuit against TP-Link Systems, alleging the router maker concealed ongoing ties to China and misled consumers about the security of its products.

title: BlackRock's Record Asset Holdings Are Half The Size Of US Economy
desc:
BlackRock's Record Asset Holdings Are Half The Size Of US Economy

BlackRock ended the third quarter with $15.49 trillion in assets under management, a record, after $205 billion of net client inflows, according to its earnings release filed with the SEC on Oct. 14.

GAAP earnings came to $10.57 a share, and as-adjusted earnings to $15.93. Revenue rose 19 percent to $7.75 billion, and the company said it has raised $68 billion in private markets over the last twelve months. Its AI Infrastructure Partnership made its first deployment during the quarter.

Chairman and CEO Larry Fink said clients "entrusted us with $205 billion of net inflows this quarter, and $869 billion over the last year." He added: "We're entering our seasonally strongest fourth quarter with accelerating momentum."

As the Epoch Times notes further, the company drew almost $135 billion in net new flows into its flagship iShares exchange-traded funds, also known as ETFs.

It also repurchased $550 million of its shares during the quarter, delivering stronger value to current shareholders.

"Market fundamentals are strong and well supported, with higher margins and earnings momentum catalyzed by new technology," CEO Larry Fink said in a statement.

Looking ahead to the final three months of 2026, Fink noted that BlackRock has plenty of momentum and a broad pipeline of opportunities across multiple business segments, including private markets and retirement funds.

BlackRock popped as much as 5 percent following the earnings data but erased its gains as the midweek session progressed.

Private Credit Improvements

The private credit industry has been under tremendous strain this year, reflecting the so-called "SaaSpocalypse" and increasing concerns surrounding lenders' exposure to software companies.

This was observed in the wave of redemption requests.

But BlackRock's push into private credit markets does not seem affected by the sector's widespread pressures.

In a call with analysts, CFO Martin Small suggested that investment demand for private credit has been solid.

Net inflows into its private credit funds rose by $5 billion from the previous quarter, according to the earnings report.

"We think there's a much larger opportunity that's more durable in delivering private high-grade private credit in for debt across our platform and just deepening our client relationships over time," Small said.

Additionally, BlackRock's client redemptions, which have been in focus for the broader industry since the start of 2026, have eased modestly.

Redemption requests for its Corporate Lending Fund fell to about 11.5 percent of shares in the latest quarter, down from 13.3 percent in the second quarter.

But while private credit stress appears to be dissipating, Moody's warned the situation could be worse than reported default rates suggest.

"Asset quality risks are mounting among weaker middle market borrowers in the US private credit market as higher-for-longer interest rates, refinancing challenges, redemption pressures and persistent concerns over transparency weigh on performance," the firm said in an Oct. 14 report.

Earnings Season So Far

Third-quarter earnings season started on Oct. 13, beginning with some of the big banks.

Tuesday's results were mixed but not concerning, says Tom Essaye, president and co-founder of The Sevens Research Report.

"The results of those earnings were mixed, but none of the reports provided the type of surprise that would have impacted the broader market and the S&P 500," Essaye said in a note emailed to The Epoch Times.

Oct. 14 was better, with Morgan Stanley, Progressive, and State Street beating Wall Street expectations on earnings per share.

Blackstone will be the next major investment manager to release its performance from the past three months.

The consensus estimate points to $1.46 in earnings per share and $3.65 billion in revenue, according to Trading Economics.

title: Guilfoyle Hit With Defamation Suit By Donor Behind $100,000 Amex Allegations
desc:
Guilfoyle Hit With Defamation Suit By Donor Behind $100,000 Amex Allegations

Trump donor Eric Deters has sued Kimberly Guilfoyle and her lawyers for defamation, escalating the dispute over an alleged $100,000 American Express payment request that preceded her departure as U.S. ambassador to Greece. Deters announced in a Thursday Facebook post that he filed in Kentucky state court. The defendants include attorneys Jesse Binnall and David M. Schwartz, CBS News reported.

Deters had previewed the lawsuit in a CNN interview Monday, accusing Guilfoyle's camp of falsely dismissing his text messages as fabricated, branding him a blackmailer and claiming he owed her money.

The filing comes two days after Guilfoyle resigned at the White House's request amid multiple reports of alleged misconduct. She has denied wrongdoing and pledged to defend her reputation. Her attorneys maintain that the financial dispute concerns unpaid compensation, not the sale of political access.

The $100,000 Request

The controversy erupted after The Wall Street Journal reported that Guilfoyle sought a $100,000 payment directly to American Express while preparing for her Senate confirmation hearing last year. The newspaper reviewed Signal messages in which she discussed helping Deters obtain administration attention for legal and tax matters.

"It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express," she wrote, according to the Journal.

Deters was not simply an outside observer complaining about Washington's influence business. In a Tuesday CNN interview, he said he had paid Guilfoyle $300,000 for speaking appearances and offered her $1 million if she helped with his medical-malpractice litigation, payable when the case settled.

He said he wanted help securing the extradition of a doctor accused of performing unnecessary spinal surgeries, along with an investigation into how the doctor left the country. Deters said Guilfoyle failed to deliver the assistance he sought.

Guilfoyle's Defense: Unpaid Fees, Not Paid Access

Guilfoyle's lawyers tell a substantially different story: Deters was a delinquent client, and she was trying to collect money for work already performed.

In an October 10 statement, Binnall and Schwartz said Deters still owed approximately $150,000 for speeches and consulting services. They cited a May 20, 2024 agreement with a third-party booking agency providing for a $200,000 fee, alongside additional speaking and consulting arrangements.

The attorneys said Deters made partial payments but failed to settle the balance, and that Guilfoyle sought to resolve outstanding payments before entering government service.

"Asking a client to pay for work already done is not corruption. It is the opposite of corruption."

They also said Guilfoyle refused Deters' separate $1 million offer and indicated they were evaluating legal remedies to collect the alleged debt.

Deters disputes that explanation. In the Tuesday interview, he denied owing Guilfoyle money and said he had been willing to describe the arrangement on paper as payment for prior consulting, while insisting that description was false.

That leaves a consequential dispute over what the money was actually for. The contracts, payment records and communications matter more than either side's public characterization. The defamation lawsuit does not, by itself, establish that the alleged pay-for-access arrangement occurred.

Deters Eyes Trump's Inner Circle

Deters is also presenting the lawsuit as a way to pull people close to the president into the dispute.

In his announcement, he said he intends to pursue depositions of Guilfoyle and her former fiance, Donald Trump Jr., and seek administration documents through subpoenas. Those are his stated intentions, not confirmation that the testimony has been scheduled or ordered.

Then came the promised bombshell. According to Mediaite, Deters said he would release a 16-minute telephone recording by the end of Friday, October 16, suggesting it could have repercussions far beyond the former ambassador.

"This might just bring down the entire Trump administration," he said. He also suggested the recording could damage the political prospects of Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, while saying he still supports the administration's policies.

title: NOAA Winter Outlook: Record El Niño Points To Wetter South, Warmer North
desc:
NOAA Winter Outlook: Record El Niño Points To Wetter South, Warmer North

El Niño is a warm patch of water in the equatorial Pacific that shows up every few years and confuses everyone as to what it's actually going to do. When the eastern Pacific runs hot, the jet stream drops south and drags the storm track with it. That is why a water temperature reading off South America decides whether California floods and the Gulf gets hammered.

NOAA's winter outlook, released this morning, favors a wetter than average December through February across the southern U.S., from California to Florida, and along the Eastern Seaboard, with warmer than average temperatures across the North.

It expects drought to improve or end in the Southwest, the southern Great Plains, the Southeast and parts of the East Coast, and to develop or worsen in parts of the northern Rockies, northeastern Oregon and eastern Washington. "As we know from decades of observations, a very strong El Nino will likely bring a southward and eastward shift to the jet stream for the contiguous U.S., which tilts the odds toward stormier weather across the South," said National Weather Service director Ken Graham, who warned that "too much precipitation on dry soil can fuel destructive flash floods and mudslides." Like every NOAA seasonal outlook, it gives the odds of a wetter or drier, warmer or colder season, and it doesn't project snowfall.

The Climate Prediction Center's three-month outlook for January through March, also issued today, carries the same pattern into spring: wetter than average from California and the Southwest across the Gulf Coast and up the East Coast, with the strongest odds in Southern California and along the Florida and Georgia coast, and warmer than average across the northern tier from the Pacific Northwest to New England. The Southeast stays near normal on temperature, and parts of Montana and Michigan lean dry.

This year's reading is off the charts. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center said Oct 8 that El Niño is still strengthening, with better than 83% odds of a strong to very strong event through early next year, and an 83% chance that it tops every El Niño on record back to 1950 over October to December. On Sept 21 the daily surface temperature where El Niño forms ran more than 3°C above normal, a daily record, months before the expected peak.

What A Strong El Niño Does To An American Winter

For this winter, NOAA favors warmer than average temperatures for northern California, the Pacific Northwest, the Midwest, the Mississippi Valley and much of the East, near normal temperatures for parts of the Southeast including Florida, and drier than average conditions for parts of the northern Mountain West. That fits its review of a century of events, which found the most reliable signal is a wet Gulf Coast: wetter than average from Texas to Florida in more than 80% of El Niño winters. California is the swing state; in the two strongest events on record, 1982-83 and 1997-98, it got much more rain than usual. The Ohio Valley trends dry, and the Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies often run mild. In NOAA's words, "the stronger the episode, the more reliable the signal."

NOAA's post-mortem of the 1997-98 winter counts four weeks of nearly continuous storms in California, 35 counties declared federal disaster areas and more than $550 million in damage. Santa Barbara took 21.74 inches of rain in February alone. In Florida, a two-day tornado outbreak killed 42 people. Nationwide the winter claimed 56 lives, and a Northeast ice storm left power lines down for weeks.

Forecasters are already split on where this one hits hardest. Meteorologist Ryan Hall is watching a corridor from Oklahoma and Arkansas through Tennessee, Kentucky, Virginia and the Carolinas: "somebody in this corridor is going to get a big snowstorm or a big ice storm this winter." AccuWeather's Paul Pastelok expects floods to matter more: "It may be more about rainfall this year."

The National Weather Service is changing its own warnings for this winter. Starting this season, select blizzard and ice storm warnings will carry "Particularly Dangerous Situation" wording, reserved for high-confidence storms of historic severity that pose "imminent danger to life and unprecedented disruptions to emergency services." NOAA updates the outlook again on Nov 19.

The Fall Was The Warm-Up

El Niño's wind shear held the Atlantic's first hurricane back about four weeks past the previous modern record. When one finally formed, it still did real damage. Hurricane Isaias came ashore near Destin, Florida, on the evening of Oct 9 with 105 mph winds and knocked out power to about 830,000 homes and businesses across Florida, Alabama and Georgia. Before landfall, producers shut in 63% of Gulf crude output and 57% of its natural gas, and WTI rose as much as 5.6% in a day.

California didn't wait for the first storm. Gov. Gavin Newsom declared a statewide emergency on Sept 21, readying the National Guard for floods and staging sandbags, pumps and road-closure equipment.

The grid is running tight going into winter. PJM Interconnection, which serves 67 million people from the Mid-Atlantic to Chicago, declared a low-level emergency this week when an October heat spike hit with 60 gigawatts of generation down for maintenance, and spot power at its western hub touched $1,021 a megawatt-hour. A PJM spokesman said "unpredictable weather patterns are providing fewer days to perform important maintenance."

The food bill comes later. JPMorgan analysts expect El Niño's biggest hit to farm output in the first quarter of 2027, on top of diesel and fertilizer shortages, and the UN Food and Agriculture Organization's chief economist told CNN global food prices were already climbing before El Niño arrived.

Recall, the numbers:

  • NOAA's winter outlook, out Oct 15, favors a wetter South and East Coast and a warmer North, and the January to March outlook keeps the same tilt.
  • NOAA gives 83% odds this El Niño tops every one on record for October through December.
  • The Gulf Coast runs wet in more than 80% of El Niño winters.
  • Isaias, the Atlantic's first and very late hurricane, still cut power to about 830,000 customers.
  • The 1997-98 event put 35 California counties under federal disaster declarations.

title: The Politics Of Denial: When Americans Stop Seeing The Warning Signs
desc:
The Politics Of Denial: When Americans Stop Seeing The Warning Signs

Authored by John & Nisha Whitehead via The Rutherford Institute,

"You see them on the street. You watch them on TV. You might even vote for one this fall. You think they're people just like you. You're wrong. Dead wrong."

- They Live

The spectacle of public executions. Deadly military strikes on foreign countries. Innocent civilian lives lost to war. Aggressive ICE raids. Government officials accused of using their powers to intimidate political opponents. Public office increasingly entangled with private financial interests. Government leaders who glorify violence, spew hatred, stir up racial prejudice, provoke civil unrest, and stoke discontent.

This is what it looks like when a nation loses its way.

When cruelty is mistaken for courage, vengeance for justice, and the taking of human life for a demonstration of strength.

When government officials tell you not to believe your own eyes and ears about the state of the world around you, when they insist that the truth is a lie and the lie is truth, you've stumbled into a dystopian reality in which, as John Lennon rightly concluded, the government is "being run by maniacs for maniacal ends."

When so-called Christians and self-professed defenders of morality insist that we must accept the lesser of two evils based on exaggerated fears of what might happen if their political opponents gain power, rather than confront the abuses unfolding before our eyes, remember this: the lesser of two evils is still evil.

This is not simply about Donald Trump.

The machinery of the American police state has been assembled over decades, under Republican and Democratic administrations alike. Presidents have expanded executive authority, waged undeclared wars, authorized drone killings, built surveillance networks, militarized domestic policing, and invoked national security to justify extraordinary powers.

What makes the present moment so troubling is the extent to which the public is encouraged to accept increasingly aggressive exercises of government power as necessary demonstrations of strength and resolve.

The Constitution was never intended to protect only the innocent, the popular, the patriotic, or the politically acceptable. Its restraints on government power matter most when the government is dealing with people whom society has already condemned.

Yet what happens when the public becomes so accustomed to government overreach, corruption and brutality that it no longer recognizes them as warning signs? What becomes of a constitutional republic when its leaders and citizens stop asking whether government actions are lawful, justified or necessary, and concern themselves only with whether those actions punish their enemies, advance their political interests or preserve their sense of security?

We are witnessing a political culture in which demanding due process for an accused criminal is treated as defending criminality, questioning a military strike is equated with sympathy for the enemy, and opposing government cruelty is portrayed as weakness.

The government doesn't have to abolish the Constitution outright when it can persuade the public that certain people should no longer be entitled to its protections.

That is how constitutional rights cease to be rights at all and become privileges granted or withdrawn at the government's discretion.

And that is how a population becomes conditioned to accept the unacceptable.

We're living in two worlds.

There's the world we see - or are made to see - and then there's the one we sense and occasionally catch a glimpse of, which bears little resemblance to the propaganda-driven reality manufactured by those in power and amplified through an increasingly fragmented media landscape.

Indeed, what most Americans perceive as life in America - privileged, progressive and free - is a far cry from the reality of a nation where economic inequality persists, government power continues to expand, and freedom is increasingly subjected to the demands of surveillance, security and control.

All is not as it seems.

Monsters with human faces walk among us.

Some of them wield extraordinary government power.

This is the premise of John Carpenter's film They Live, released in November 1988, which remains unnervingly, chillingly appropriate for our modern age.

Best known for his horror film Halloween, Carpenter's larger body of work is infused with a strong anti-authoritarian, anti-establishment, laconic bent that speaks to the filmmaker's concerns about the unraveling of our society, particularly our government.

Time and again, Carpenter portrays the government working against its own citizens, a populace out of touch with reality, technology run amok, and a future more horrific than any horror film.

In They Live, two migrant workers discover that the world is being subliminally controlled and exploited by aliens working in partnership with an oligarchic elite.

All the while, the populace - blissfully unaware of the real agenda at work in their lives - has been lulled into complacency, indoctrinated into compliance, bombarded with media distractions, and hypnotized by hidden messages beamed out of television and various electronic devices, billboards and the like.

Sound familiar?

It is only when homeless drifter John Nada, played by the late Roddy Piper, discovers a pair of special sunglasses that he sees what lies beneath the elite's fabricated reality: control and bondage.

When viewed through Nada's lenses, the wealthy and powerful who appear human are revealed as monsters exploiting the citizenry.

Likewise, seemingly mundane advertisements conceal subliminal, authoritarian messages. Magazine racks scream "CONSUME" and "OBEY." Money proclaims "THIS IS YOUR GOD." Other hidden messages reinforce the same demands: CONFORM. SUBMIT. STAY ASLEEP. WATCH TV. DO NOT QUESTION AUTHORITY. NO INDEPENDENT THOUGHT.

This indoctrination campaign engineered by the elite in They Live is painfully familiar to anyone who has studied the workings of an authoritarian state.

A citizenry that does not think for themselves, obeys without question, is submissive, does not challenge authority, does not think outside the box, and is content to sit back and be entertained is a citizenry that can be easily controlled.

In this way, the message of They Live provides an apt analogy for the distorted vision of life in the American police state - what philosopher Slavoj Žižek has characterized as the invisible structures of domination that sustain the appearance of freedom.

Tune out the government's attempts to distract, divert and befuddle us and tune into what's really going on in this country, and you'll run headlong into an uncomfortable truth: government corruption and power have expanded far beyond the restraints the Constitution was intended to impose.

And the corruption is not always hidden.

What happens when public office, private wealth and political influence become so intertwined that ordinary citizens can no longer distinguish whose interests their government is serving? What happens when those conflicts are repeatedly exposed, yet the public becomes too distracted, too divided or too politically invested to demand answers?

This is where the warning of They Live becomes especially relevant.

The danger is not simply that powerful interests might conceal what they're doing. It's that they can operate in plain sight, confident that enough people will refuse to see - or refuse to care.

We have allowed the government's corruption, brutality, self-dealing and abuses go on for too long. While this has been true of both parties, it has become painfully evident under the Trump administration.

Desperate to hold onto power, the powers-that-be continue to advance a series of carefully contrived narratives, threats and emergencies to justify expanding their authority, encouraging the public to fear one another, distrust our own judgment, and accept increasingly invasive government powers as the price of safety.

Fear is the great enabler of authoritarianism.

Fear of terrorists. Fear of criminals. Fear of immigrants. Fear of foreign enemies. Fear of domestic extremists. Fear of one another.

Every new threat becomes another justification for expanding government authority, weakening constitutional safeguards, and demanding greater obedience from a frightened public.

This is how government power expands in plain sight. The targets are portrayed as threats. The government's actions are defended as necessary. Those who question its methods are accused of defending criminals, undermining public safety or siding with the enemy.

And with every exception made to constitutional restraints, the public becomes a little more accustomed to powers it once would have considered intolerable. Surveillance becomes security. Censorship becomes protection. Militarized policing becomes public safety. Indefinite detention becomes national defense.

And killing becomes justice.

For too long, Americans have been persuaded to barter their freedoms for promises of security, rationalizing government wrongdoing because they are told the alternatives would be worse.

But no matter how you rationalize it, the lesser of two evils is still evil.

The greatest danger is not merely that government officials may abuse their power.

It is that ordinary people may become so accustomed to those abuses that they lose the ability - or the willingness - to recognize them for what they are.

This brings us back to They Live, in which the danger posed is not simply the alien conspiracy but the population's willingness to remain asleep and controlled.

Again, not so different from our own.

As one of the characters points out, "The poor and the underclass are growing. Racial justice and human rights are nonexistent. They have created a repressive society and we are their unwitting accomplices. Their intention to rule rests with the annihilation of consciousness. We have been lulled into a trance. They have made us indifferent to ourselves, to others. We are focused only on our own gain."

We, too, are encouraged to focus on our own pleasures, prejudices and political victories, while remaining indifferent to the suffering of others. Our poor and underclasses are also growing. Injustice is growing. Inequality is growing. A concern for human rights is nearly nonexistent. We too have been lulled into a trance, indifferent to others.

The government doesn't have to convince everyone that its actions are lawful, just or humane. It merely has to persuade enough people that those being targeted deserve whatever happens to them.

Nor does corruption have to be concealed when it can be rationalized, dismissed, or excused as the unavoidable cost of keeping one's preferred political leaders in power.

This is perhaps the most disturbing parallel to They Live: a population that has been shown what is happening, yet remains unwilling to confront the implications.

The warning signs are no longer buried beneath elaborate disguises. They are unfolding in courtrooms, detention facilities, government offices, financial disclosures and daily news reports.

And still, too many people choose to look away.

We can convince ourselves that we are different from the victims of government abuse. That we are too law-abiding, too patriotic, too respectable, too insignificant to become targets ourselves.

We can tell ourselves that the government means well, that extraordinary measures are necessary, and that those caught in the machinery of state power must have done something to deserve their fate. But every exception made to someone else's rights weakens the protections intended to safeguard our own.

That was the warning behind the Bill of Rights.

The founders understood that government officials could not be trusted to restrain themselves simply because they professed good intentions. The Constitution was intended to bind government power, not magnify it.

So where does that leave us?

The characters who populate Carpenter's films provide some insight.

Underneath their machismo, they still believe in the ideals of liberty and equal opportunity. Their beliefs place them in constant opposition with the law and the establishment, but they are nonetheless freedom fighters.

When John Nada destroys the alien hypno-transmitter in They Live, he delivers a wake-up call for freedom. As Nada memorably declares, "I have come here to chew bubblegum and kick ass. And I'm all out of bubblegum."

In other words, it's time to get active and take a stand for what's really important.

Stop allowing yourselves to be easily distracted by political spectacles and manufactured fears. Stop treating constitutional rights as privileges reserved for people you agree with. Stop excusing government abuses merely because the victims are unpopular or the perpetrators share your political loyalties.

As we make clear in Battlefield America: The War on the American People and its fictional counterpart The Erik Blair Diaries, all the trappings of the American police state are now in plain sight.

The greatest danger is not that the monsters have become so adept at hiding among us. It is that we have become so conditioned to their presence, so accustomed to their abuses, and so willing to excuse their corruption that we no longer recognize them for what they are.

Wake up, America.

If they live - the tyrants, the oppressors, the invaders, the overlords - it is only because "we the people" sleep.

title: 57 California Dams In Poor Or Unsatisfactory Condition, State Auditor Says
desc:
57 California Dams In Poor Or Unsatisfactory Condition, State Auditor Says

Authored by Naveen Athrappully via The Epoch Times,

A new report from the state auditor says 57 dams in California are in poor or unsatisfactory condition, posing a safety risk to hundreds of thousands of residents.

Out of those 57 dams, 40 have "high or extremely high" hazard classifications as of May, the Oct. 13 report said.

"Failure of just one of these 40 high or extremely high hazard dams could pose harm to as many as hundreds of thousands of people and cause billions of dollars in property damage," the auditor warned, citing the Department of Water Resources' (DWR's) assessment of 1,222 Californian dams.

The most common factors for the poor conditions are old age, the inability to pay for repair costs, and the lack of comprehensive safety standards in effect when the dams were built, the report said.

While the DWR has enforcement authority over dams, it has "only sent notices of violations to dam owners but has not taken further actions, thereby allowing serious deficiencies to persist," the auditor said.

The department stated that limited resources hindered efforts to repair dams before they failed.

Of the 1,222 dams, the auditor found that owners of 60 dams with higher hazard classifications did not comply with California law requiring they submit emergency action plans aimed at protecting life and property in case of structure failure.

Local maintaining agencies (LMAs) were charged with maintenance of levees - structures that help contain or control water flow during floods.

In the report, the auditor wrote that LMAs were lacking when it came to levee maintenance, while the DWR was reluctant to intervene, posing heightened risks to communities.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom proclaimed an emergency last month to prepare the state for El Niño, when southern areas of the state face increased rainfall and flash flooding.

The largest impacts of El Niño typically affect the United States from October through May.

In the emergency declaration, Newsom highlighted the risks posed to dams by El Niño conditions.

In the proclamation, Newsom ordered the DWR to contact dam owners and remind them of their responsibility to repair, maintain, and safely manage dams and other structures.

Meanwhile, the California state auditor's report included a response from the DWR regarding the draft version of the document.

The response criticized the audit report for portraying a "fundamental lack of understanding" of the complexities involved in flood management and dam safety.

The DWR said the audit misrepresents that poor maintenance and lack of action are the sole reasons for dams being in unsatisfactory condition.

"This further demonstrates the lack of technical understanding that the most critical deficiencies are found through DWR's reevaluation program; these are not visible in an inspection and most often occur because design loads (earthquakes and floods) are larger than originally expected," the department said.

"Design standards, engineering methods, and science have changed over time. These dams were not necessarily built poorly."

The DWR's reevaluation program periodically reviews dams deemed to pose a threat to life against current dam safety standards.

The department said that the program is responsible for detecting more than two-thirds of dam deficiencies.

In a Sept. 30 statement, the DWR announced completing a $235 million rehabilitation of California's Oroville Dam, the tallest in the United States.

"This investment in Oroville Dam's infrastructure ensures the reliable and safe operation of the State Water Project's largest flood protection and water supply facility," John Yarbrough, deputy director of the DWR's State Water Project, said in the statement.

Dam safety is a wider national issue as well.

According to a report from the American Society of Civil Engineers, almost 17,000 dams in the United States are considered potentially high hazard.

The report highlighted that the average age of dams in the United States is more than 60 years, with seven out of 10 estimated to be at least 50 years old in 2025.

"Without a more significant commitment to dam safety through increased annual investment in inspection, monitoring, planning, and necessary dam repairs, the cost to bring the nation's dams into a state of good repair will continue to rise," the association said.

"And downstream communities will face a greater risk of danger from potential dam failure."

The U.S. Department of Justice on Oct. 13 sent letters to California election officials demanding a review within 48 hours of registered voters it suspects are noncitizens and asking officials to set aside their mail ballots until their citizenship status can be determined.

"Accompanying this letter is a password-protected thumb drive with a list of names of people the Federal Government believes are likely noncitizens who were sent a vote-by-mail ballot from California to participate in the November election," the letter stated.

The letter requested that L.A. County review the list within 48 hours. For any individuals the county could not independently verify as citizens, the letter requested election officials be instructed to "segregate - not cancel" those vote-by-mail ballots until their citizenship status could be determined.

If the county didn't comply with the DOJ request, the letter stated, "the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief."

"Maintaining accurate voter registration records is a fundamental responsibility of our office," Logan said in a statement. The California Secretary of State also criticized the DOJ's letter in a response on X.

"The US DOJ's relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections," the statement said. title: Think Rates Are Peaking? Consider Mortgage-Backed Securities
desc:
Think Rates Are Peaking? Consider Mortgage-Backed Securities

Authored by Michael Lebowitz via RealInvestmentAdvice.com,

Think interest rates are peaking? If so, agency mortgage-backed securities (MBS) deserve a look. Think rates have further to climb? MBS may still earn a place in your fixed-income allocation, potentially offering more yield than Treasuries and essentially no credit risk.

Here is the twist. In 2022 and 2023, MBS investors learned a painful lesson. As rates surged, homeowners stopped refinancing, and MBS durations rose at the worst possible time. Today, that dynamic has largely run its course. With 30-year mortgage rates at 7.25% and nearly 80% of homeowners holding a rate below 6%, refinancing has all but stopped, leaving MBS durations little room to extend further. The feature that hurt MBS investors in 2022 and 2023 has little room for further harm.

MBS are a unique type of bond because mortgagees can prepay part or all of their mortgage at any time without penalty. Thus, MBS investors, who have essentially lent mortgagees money, are, inherently, short a prepayment option. The prepayment option accounts for much of the extra yield MBS offer over Treasuries, as well as their greater interest rate risk. But when the risks are limited, MBS holders are often in an advantageous position.

In this article, we weigh the pros and cons of MBS at current yields, explain what will drive future returns, and share how individual investors can gain exposure.

Setting The Stage

Mortgage rates and Treasury yields have moved sharply higher over the last six months. Per Freddie Mac, the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.28% as of October 1, the highest since November 2023, and up from 6.34% a year ago.

Source: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey, via Real Investment Advice

The graph above shows that virtually all mortgages originated from the early 2000s have a rate below the current rate. Accordingly, refinancing activity has dried up. To wit, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) reported that its refinance index is over 50% below the same level a year ago. Per Joel Kan of the MBA:

Mortgage rates jumped to their highest level in almost three years, pushing borrowers to the sidelines.

The iShares MBS ETF (MBB), a reasonable proxy for the agency MBS index, holds securities with a weighted average coupon of 3.63%, roughly 3.50% below the current mortgage rate. With most mortgages at least 2% below current rates, very few homeowners have an economic reason to refinance.

In bond terminology, their prepayment option is worth little. To better understand why this matters for MBS investors, let's focus on MBS duration.

Understanding MBS Duration

Duration measures a bond's price sensitivity to changes in interest rates. A bond with a duration of seven years should lose about 7% of its value if yields rise by 1% and gain about 7% if yields fall by 1%. For Treasury, municipal, and corporate bonds, duration is fairly predictable because their interest and principal cash flows are fixed.

MBS investor cash flows depend on when and by how much homeowners pay down their mortgages, which depends largely on interest rates. Therefore, changes in interest rates have a much more profound impact on MBS durations than Treasury and corporate durations.

MBS investors track effective duration, a model-based duration estimate that accounts for how prepayments are expected to change as rates move.

  • When rates rise, refinancing slows, cash flows are pushed further into the future, and duration lengthens.
  • When rates fall, refinancing accelerates, principal comes back sooner, and duration shortens.

The graph below shows a hypothetical comparison of MBS and Treasury duration for a range of Treasury yield levels. Note how quickly MBS duration changes when rates are between 4% and 6%. At the same time, note the relatively flat, downward-sloping Treasury duration once rates are above 6%. The lower graph shows that refinancing activity is highly sensitive to rate changes when 10-year Treasury yields are in the 4% to 6% range.

Source: Real Investment Advice (illustrative model, not market data)

Coping With Duration Shifts - Negative Convexity

The graph above shows that MBS rate exposure tends to shift in the wrong direction at the wrong time for investors. For instance:

  • Duration increases when yields rise, so price losses are greater than they would have been if duration had remained constant.
  • Duration declines when falling rates would otherwise produce larger price gains had duration remained constant.

Those negative consequences are called negative convexity.

This all means that the stated duration of an MBS or portfolio of MBS is a snapshot, not a constant. Investors should expect it to change as rates change and watch where current mortgage rates sit relative to the point at which homeowners can profitably refinance.

Extension Risk Is Largely Spent

Extension risk, or rising duration, has been harming MBS investors since rates started rising in late 2021. As rates rise, refinancing slows, the expected life of the mortgage pool lengthens, and duration increases precisely when investors least want more duration. MBS holders acutely felt the negative convexity in 2022 and 2023.

Today, despite the recent rate increase, much of that extension has already occurred. When a mortgage pool is deeply out of the money, or not economically refinanceable, as many are today, prepayments are driven almost entirely by factors unrelated to interest rates such as:

  • Home sales.
  • Scheduled amortization of principal.
  • Defaults, which, for agency MBS, return principal at par.
  • Cash-out refinancing, which is limited at current rates.

These and other sources of principal repayment create a floor under prepayment speeds.

Today, prepayments can't slow much more; thus, further rate increases would not extend duration much. Put differently, MBS investors buying today are taking on duration that is relatively capped on the upside. Accordingly, the risk/reward for MBS looks more balanced than it did a few years ago.

The Con: The Double Whammy If Rates Fall

The flip side of limited duration extension risk is the MBS problem when rates decline. If mortgage rates fall meaningfully, higher-coupon pools face two penalties at once:

  • Principal earning higher rates returned through prepayments must be reinvested at lower rates.
  • Duration shortens. As refinancing accelerates, the expected life of the MBS declines, capping price appreciation relative to a comparable Treasury.

This is the cost of the prepayment option MBS investors essentially sold to homeowners. The extra yield they earn over Treasuries is the premium they are paid for bearing it.

The Silver Lining To The Double Whammy

Within the double whammy, i.e., negative convexity, lies a potential reward in today's market. If mortgage rates fall by almost 2.5% to 5%, over two-thirds of mortgages, as we share below, have no financial incentive to refinance.

Source: Redfin analysis of FHFA National Mortgage Database (Q3 2025); Freddie Mac PMMS, via Real Investment Advice

For most of the MBS market, falling rates in the recent environment are a good thing:

  • Because refinancing will be slow to kick in, duration declines should be minimal; investors can capture a large amount of the price benefit of lower yields.
  • Faster prepayments become a gain. Lower rates tend to boost home sales, and every sale pays off a loan at par. For MBS trading below par, each dollar returned early is profit pulled forward.

Bear in mind it's not just the low number of high-rate loans that will likely limit prepays when rates fall. Refinancing takes months for borrowers to notice lower rates, shop lenders, and close loans. Furthermore, given the lack of recent refinancing and home sale activity, lender capacity could become a bottleneck if applications surge.

Also, many borrowers never refinance. Some lack the credit score or home equity to qualify, some have balances too small to justify closing costs, and others simply do not act. As a result, investors continue to collect above-market coupons on the loans that remain.

Falling rates can be very beneficial to MBS holders given today's backdrop.

How To Invest In MBS

For institutional investors, the agency MBS market is one of the deepest and most liquid fixed income markets in the world. Owning individual MBS is ideal in theory. It allows investors to choose the coupon, vintage, and prepayment characteristics that best fit their views. However, in practice, it is challenging and impractical for smaller investors for the following reasons:

  • Pools factor down. Every month, a portion of principal is returned. A $100,000 position may be $60,000 within a few years, and small, "odd-lot" positions trade at meaningful discounts to larger pools.
  • Monthly principal must be reinvested. Small, irregular cash flows are difficult to put back to work efficiently.
  • Prepayment analysis requires data and models most individual investors do not have.
  • Dealer access and pricing transparency for small trades are limited.

For these reasons, an ETF or mutual fund may be a more practical option for smaller investors. Funds handle reinvestment, maintain diversification across coupons and vintages, and benefit from professional management, institutional models, and lower trading costs.

Passive ETFs such as MBB offer broad index exposure at low cost; its expense ratio is 0.04%. Actively managed MBS funds, such as JMBS, can shift their holdings toward coupons and specified pools that managers believe offer better convexity profiles, albeit at higher fees.

Investors should review a fund's coupon distribution, effective duration, and use of leverage or derivatives. Two funds with similar durations can behave differently.

The graphic below compares the most popular passive MBS ETF, MBB, to the largest active ETF, JMBS.

Source: iShares, Janus Henderson fund pages (as of Oct 5, 2026), via Real Investment Advice

Summary- Investment Thesis

A bullish thesis rests on two key points. First, interest rates stabilize and start to fall.

Second, even if rates rise, the duration shift is largely capped, as the graph below shows. Accordingly, assuming MBS-to-Treasury spreads do not change, the price change between an MBS and a similar-maturity Treasury will not be that indifferent.

Three years ago, extension risk was the reason to avoid MBS. Today, it is one reason to own them. With most mortgages far below market rates, MBS duration has little room left to extend or refinance. Investors are left with an asset class that offers high yields, minimal credit risk, and stable duration.

title: US Issues First Outbound Investment Penalty Over Chinese Robotics AI Deal
desc:
US Issues First Outbound Investment Penalty Over Chinese Robotics AI Deal

Authored by Arthur Zhang via The Epoch Times,

The U.S. Treasury Department has fined Amidi LLC $200,000 for failing to report an investment in a Chinese tech startup - the first penalty under U.S. restrictions on investments in sensitive Chinese technologies.

Amidi is the parent company of Plug and Play Tech Center, a California-based venture investment and startup accelerator organization. The Treasury imposed the penalty in July and disclosed it on Oct. 7.

According to Treasury, a Chinese investment fund controlled by Amidi invested $92,478 on April 19, 2025, in Shanghai Qiongche Intelligent Technology, known as Noematrix, a Shanghai-based developer of AI technology that helps robots interact with and perform tasks in the physical world.

The Treasury identified the transaction through regular compliance and market monitoring. The violation was a failure to report the investment, not a finding that the investment itself was prohibited.

1st Penalty Under US Investment Restrictions

The Outbound Investment Security Program, which took effect on Jan. 2, 2025, prohibits certain U.S. investments in Chinese companies developing advanced artificial intelligence, semiconductors, and quantum technologies. Other transactions involving these sectors are permitted but require notification to the Treasury.

The rules also cover certain investments made through foreign subsidiaries controlled by American companies.

The restrictions are intended to prevent American capital and investment-related benefits from supporting the development of sensitive technologies that could threaten U.S. national security.

Christopher Pilkerton, the Treasury's assistant secretary for investment security, said in the Oct. 7 announcement that the program addresses the development of sensitive technologies by countries of concern that could pose national security risks.

Plug and Play's China Investment Network

Amidi's investment in Noematrix followed several earlier financing rounds involving Plug and Play China, the China-based investment and startup development operation of the Silicon Valley network.

Noematrix identified Plug and Play China as an investor in its September 2024 financing, several months before the U.S. restrictions took effect.

In December 2024, Noematrix announced another financing round led by Sequoia China, a Chinese venture capital firm, and said Plug and Play China had increased its investment.

On April 10, 2025, Noematrix announced another financing round, again naming Plug and Play China as a participating investor.

Nine days later, the Amidi-controlled Chinese fund made the investment identified in the Treasury's enforcement action. It remains unclear whether the two transactions were connected or whether the fund was the investment vehicle used by Plug and Play China.

The Epoch Times contacted the Treasury, Amidi, Noematrix, and Plug and Play China to seek clarification on the Chinese fund, its relationship with the Silicon Valley investment network, and the failure to notify U.S. authorities. None responded by publication time.

Chinese University and State-Linked Investment

Noematrix has since received financing from Chinese university-linked and state-owned investors.

In June 2026, the company announced another financing round involving Shanghai Jiao Tong University's AI Future Fund, a university-linked technology investment fund; Shanghai Chuangzhi Technology, a subsidiary of the Shanghai Chuangzhi Academy research institution; and Wuxi Data Group, a state-owned data industry company.

Noematrix said it had worked with Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Shanghai Chuangzhi Academy on joint laboratories and research projects. Its co-founder Lu Cewu is a professor and vice dean of Shanghai Jiao Tong University's School of Artificial Intelligence.

The company also said it had joined Wuxi Data Group and other partners in launching a citywide initiative to collect high-quality data from real-world activities to train robotic AI systems.

The initiative targets data from 1,000 businesses and 1 million hours of real-world activity, according to Noematrix. The company said the partners had released the project's first phase results and planned to expand industrial datasets to support the use of AI-powered robots on production lines.

"Worst Is Yet To Come": Global Smartphone Shipments Crash 22% As Memory Crisis Squeezes Consumers

Technology research firm IDC's latest report confirms our warning earlier this week of "more pain to come," with global smartphone shipments plunging in the third quarter as rising memory chip costs squeeze margins, boost handset prices, and make these devices more expensive than ever.

Preliminary data from the advisory firm show worldwide smartphone shipments plunged 22% year over year to 255.3 million units in the third quarter, as the AI-related memory chip shortage sent component costs soaring, forcing manufacturers to raise prices beyond consumers' comfort zones.

"The sharp downturn the industry has been bracing for finally materialized in the third quarter this year, with shipments declining a record 22% YoY. However, the worst is yet to come," senior IDC research director Nabila Popal wrote in the report released earlier this morning.

Popal said, "Memory costs have surged approximately 350% since last year and are still rising, creating substantial pressure on vendor margins and shipments. While memory inflation is beginning to slow down, with a low double-digit sequential increase in Q3 compared to roughly 50%-100% sequential growth in prior quarters, costs remain elevated across other critical components as well, compounding the crunch."

IDC expects handset shipment growth to remain under pressure through 2027, with any recovery pushed to 2028 at the earliest. Manufacturers increasingly view the cost shock as a permanent change in the industry's economics.

This cost shock has hit Chinese brands hardest, which are highly exposed to budget markets, as soaring chip costs have squeezed margins and price increases now risk driving customers away. Conversely, Apple and Samsung are gaining market share, as their premium handset portfolios and supply advantages help shield them from the downturn.

IDC vice president Francisco Jeronimo wrote in the report, "The third quarter shows the full impact and damage of the memory crisis," adding, "The pressure is now moving from vendors to consumers. As higher prices reach the shelf, many buyers are keeping their current devices longer. Chinese brands face a particularly difficult moment, as their exposure to low-end smartphones forces them to choose between protecting margins and defending volume just as demand weakens. Volumes will stay under pressure in the coming quarters, while vendors with scale, secure supply and a premium mix keep gaining share in a smaller market."

IDC's report was in line with Loop Capital analyst John Donovan's report earlier this week, which said global smartphone shipments tumbled 22% in the third quarter. Like IDC, Donovan warned that there is a lot "more pain to come.

title: Lisa Cook's Attorney Challenges Fairness Of White House Probe
desc:
Lisa Cook's Attorney Challenges Fairness Of White House Probe

Authored by Matthew Vadum via The Epoch Times,

Federal Reserve board member Lisa Cook's attorney called into question the fairness and objectivity of a White House probe after President Donald Trump announced a new committee to investigate whether Cook made false statements.

In an Oct. 13 letter to White House counsel William Scharf obtained by The Epoch Times, lawyer Abbe Lowell wrote that one proposed member of the committee that will review the allegations against Cook, White House economic policy adviser Kevin Hassett, had previously pressed Cook to go on leave from her office and said Trump had "cause" to fire her.

A year ago, Hassett said Cook's refusal to step aside was "a partisan stance contrary to the independence of the Fed." Lowell said this comment suggests that he has prejudged the case.

The White House has proposed a Nov. 5 in-person hearing with Cook.

"A hearing with demonstrably biased members, unspecified additional allegations, and an unclear schedule for the disclosure of any additional evidence - with no explanation for why it was not previously produced - is not a process that respects the appearance or history of independence" of the Fed, Lowell wrote.

These are some of the issues that would have to be addressed before a hearing could take place, he said.

The Oct. 13 letter from Lowell comes days after Trump unveiled the new committee to investigate whether Cook made false statements.

The committee will probe allegations that Cook provided false information in connection with at least one mortgage instrument, Trump said in a presidential memorandum establishing the panel.

Trump later told reporters he would fire Cook if the committee were to recommend it. Cook's attorneys have said a fair hearing would demonstrate that the president has no legal basis for firing her.

Lowell said Cook will not be able to appear at the November hearing because she will be in Europe attending financial and monetary policy meetings. The earliest she is available is after the Fed's policy meeting set for Dec. 8 and Dec. 9, he said.

On June 29, the Supreme Court blocked the firing, rejecting Trump's arguments that he could avoid judicial review. The 5-4 decision said Cook was "entitled to notice and some opportunity to respond before her termination."

The ruling outlined a path for possibly removing Cook if she were given a chance to review the evidence and afforded an opportunity to refute it, which appears to be the path the White House is pursuing.

Trump said he followed the provisions of the Federal Reserve Act, which he said permits presidents to remove board members "for cause."

White House spokesperson Matthew Middleton defended the process, saying the Constitution requires the president to ensure that laws are followed and that the conduct of Fed governors "is above reproach."

"The President is going beyond what the Supreme Court required by offering Lisa Cook an in-person hearing that will be conducted in a fair and open process," he told The Epoch Times.

A White House official said the committee will consist of a senior economist and expert on the Federal Reserve, an employment law expert, and an expert in government ethics. Cook's hearing will be on the record, and she will be allowed to be represented by an attorney. She will be given the evidence in advance and will have an opportunity to present her own written evidence, as well as written witness statements, the official said.

President Joe Biden appointed Cook as one of the Federal Reserve's board members in 2022 and reappointed her in 2023. Both times, Cook was confirmed by the U.S. Senate.

title: Nord Stream Sabotage Trial Begins With Explosive Allegations Against Ukraine
desc:
Nord Stream Sabotage Trial Begins With Explosive Allegations Against Ukraine

Authored by RFE/RL staff via OilPrice.com,

  • A German court is trying former Ukrainian officer Serhii Kuznetsov over his alleged role in coordinating the September 2022 Nord Stream pipeline sabotage.

  • German prosecutors allege the operation was conducted on behalf of Ukrainian state authorities, although Kyiv denies involvement and no Ukrainian political leadership role has been established.

  • The trial could intensify political disputes in Germany over continued military assistance to Ukraine, particularly among opposition parties critical of Berlin's support.

After four years of speculation, leaks, and briefings by anonymous sources, the world is finally about to hear evidence given publicly under oath in a German courtroom about how the Nord Stream gas pipelines were blown up - in a case that could prove politically explosive.

German prosecutors have identified seven Ukrainian suspects, but just one of them is in the dock in the trial beginning on October 14. He is named as Serhii K. in court documents that say he is suspected of being an accomplice to a war crime.

That classification has caused outrage. But German prosecutors have further raised the stakes by stating the suspects were operating "on behalf of state authorities in Ukraine."

Kyiv has always strictly denied any involvement in the attack, which damaged crucial energy infrastructure serving Germany - one of its most important military backers in its fight since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Serhii K., who has been identified elsewhere as Serhiy Kuznetsov, says he is innocent.

'Two Crazy Military Men'

Nord Stream is majority-owned by Russia's state-controlled Gazprom and co-financed by major European energy companies. It was constructed to deliver Russian gas directly to Germany, bypassing transit states such as Ukraine and Poland, which had tense relations with Moscow.

The suspected sabotage and subsequent gas leaks happened in September 2022, rendering the pipelines as inoperable.

Western governments originally accused Russia of carrying out the blasts, but German investigators started forming a case that said a group of Ukrainian divers hired a yacht and planted explosives on the seabed.

They say Kuznetsov, a former military officer, was the ringleader.

"At the end of February 2022, he and other military personnel, on behalf of state authorities in Ukraine, developed the plan," says a summary of the indictment released by prosecutors. "The aim was to permanently halt gas deliveries via the pipelines and prevent Russia from using the revenue from the natural gas trade to finance its war efforts."

The prosecutors have not stated publicly the full extent of the alleged conspiracy.

The full indictment contains some further details, according to three German media outlets that say they have seen it: public-service TV station ARD and two print-era heavyweights, Sueddeutsche Zeitung and Die Zeit.

They all reported that, while in custody in Italy, Kuznetsov had phoned his wife in Kyiv and investigators were secretly listening in as he said he'd been advised by a lawyer that it was time to admit this had been "an official military operation." His commander should state that they were not just "two crazy military men."

Kuznetsov's Italian lawyer, Nicola Canestrini, has played down the importance of this evidence, saying there was "no smoking gun" in the case.

"It is hard to believe that, after Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, a German court should hold a war crimes trial against a Ukrainian serviceman," he added in comments to RFE/RL.

The three German media outlets named Roman Chervinskiy as Serhii K.'s commander, and his name also appeared in multiple earlier media reports citing intelligence sources. Chervinskiy told RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service in July that "the Germans actually have no evidence whatsoever that Serhii took part in this operation, if it even took place."

Another suspect, identified by Germany as Vladimir Z., is currently in custody in Croatia, where he is fighting extradition. He was previously detained in Poland but was freed when a Polish judge ruled that if Ukraine were responsible for the Nord Stream attack, it was a "just" act.

A professional diver identified by his Polish lawyers as Volodymyr Zhuravlyov, he was working in Croatia as an adviser on a Hollywood movie about Nord Stream.

During the trial, the prosecution will have to lay out its evidence for a conspiracy and the full extent of it.

"That is the crucial question: How much came from the top of the Ukrainian political system or how much was prepared by some insiders in the intelligence service?" Stefan Meister, a specialist on Russia and Eastern Europe at the German Council on Foreign Relations, told RFE/RL.

"The key political question is the role of Zelenskyy and the presidential administration. And there we still have no proof that they were really involved," he added.

Kuznetsov's German lawyer, Jes Meyer-Lohkamp, said prosecutors "have not provided any direct, conclusive evidence of our client's involvement" and that the German court will have to determine whether Nord Stream was actually a legitimate military target.

The Hanseatic Higher Regional Court in Hamburg has scheduled two hearings every week until at least February, with no specified end date yet.

German Support For Ukraine

As the case unfolds, it will also feed into bitter disputes in Germany about ongoing support for Ukraine. The main opposition party, Alternative for Germany (AfD), is highly critical of this support and calls for close ties to Russia instead.

Evidence of Ukrainian involvement in the Nord Stream attack "would strengthen the AfD's argumentation against this support for Ukraine," said Meister. "They have all these narratives about Ukrainian corruption, a failed state.... It would resonate also in parts of German society."

The AfD has recently won key regional elections and is piling the pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government over Ukraine, immigration, and economic concerns.

Merz's response has been to double down on his current policies, including on Ukraine. Most recently, he was in Kyiv on October 4 with a new aid package including joint production of interceptors to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones.

Mikhaylo Honchar, head of the Kyiv-based Strategy XXI Global Studies Center, told RFE/RL this would likely continue regardless of what comes out at the trial.

"If you take into consideration real Russian policy, which is directed against the EU and NATO, and Russia's anti-German rhetoric, I think the government of Germany will avoid steps which would undermine the bilateral relationship [with Ukraine]", he said.

He added that the prosecution case was "absurd," citing German media reports that the attack may have been a Russian false-flag operation.

But in any case, Honchar said, a guilty verdict would be met with a clear response in Ukraine. "Many people will say: 'If our guys did it, they are heroes.'"
